title: Towards Unbiased Gravitational-Wave Parameter Estimation using Score-Based Likelihood Characterization

en.text: Almost all gravitational-wave data analysis rests on a convenient fiction: that detector noise is Gaussian and stationary. The assumption is what makes the likelihood tractable and cheap to evaluate, and it has underpinned most of the last decade's parameter estimation. Real instruments are less obliging. The sensitivity of LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA drifts over time, their data are peppered with transient bursts called glitches, and narrow spectral lines wander slowly across the band.

These departures are not academic. The most famous example is the first binary neutron star merger, GW170817, which landed squarely on top of a loud glitch in a LIGO detector and required bespoke data surgery before it could be analyzed. As gravitational-wave astronomy moves into an era of large event catalogs, even small deviations from the Gaussian assumption quietly accumulate into systematic biases across thousands of signals.

This work, from the Université de Montréal, Mila, Ciela, and the Flatiron Institute, takes a different route. If real noise is hard to write down in closed form, then stop assuming it and learn it from the data instead. The authors bring a technique called Score-based Likelihood Characterization (SLIC) to gravitational-wave inference: a score-based diffusion model learns the distribution of real detector noise, which is then coupled to a differentiable physical waveform model to form an unbiased likelihood that never assumes the noise is Gaussian.

en.caption: Figure 1. Power spectral density (PSD) of synthetic noise generated by SLIC (blue), compared with a Welch estimate from real LIGO-Hanford data (dashed gray). The blue curve is drawn from 1024 synthetic segments, with the light-blue band showing the 68% interval. SLIC closely matches the real noise and, having seen more data (11 h vs 1 h), resolves the narrow spectral lines even more finely than the Welch estimate.

en.text: Paper and code: the paper is available at https://ml4astro.github.io/icml2023/assets/70.pdf and the code is open-sourced at https://github.com/RonanLegin/slicgw .
The problem: the likelihood needs a noise model, and real noise has no closed form

Extracting astrophysics from a gravitational-wave detector is a Bayesian inference problem: given a stretch of data, infer the posterior over the source parameters (black hole masses, spins, distance, and so on). That step requires a likelihood, and the shape of the likelihood is dictated entirely by the statistics of the noise. The Gaussian-stationary assumption is popular precisely because it yields a closed-form likelihood that is fast and stable to evaluate.

The catch is that the glitches, spectral lines, and subthreshold astrophysical signals in real data mostly have no ready generative model. Today they are handled segment by segment with custom fixes that are expensive and can quietly introduce bias. What the authors really want is to keep every advantage of the deterministic waveform models that standard inference relies on, while dropping the one unrealistic assumption about the detector noise.
The method: learn the score of the noise instead of assuming its form

SLIC targets a class of additive-noise inverse problems, where an observation equals a deterministic signal model plus noise: x_O = M(θ) + x. Here M(θ) is the waveform determined by the source parameters θ, and x is the noise. The key observation is that if you can obtain the score of the noise distribution Q — the gradient of its log-probability, ∇ₓ log Q(x) — then, combined with the Jacobian of the waveform model ∇θ M(θ), you can write the gradient of the likelihood with respect to the source parameters as the product below:
∇θ log p(x_O | θ) = −∇ₓ log Q(x) · ∇θ M(θ),  with  x = x_O − M(θ).

The method therefore splits in two. For the noise, a score-based diffusion model is trained with denoising score matching to learn ∇ₓ log Q(x) directly from samples of real LIGO noise, with no assumption that it is Gaussian. For the physics, the waveform is the differentiable IMRPhenomD model implemented in the ripple package, which makes automatic differentiation — and hence the Jacobian the equation needs — possible. Multiplying the two gives the score of the likelihood, and the authors draw posterior samples from it using a Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA). The framework was originally developed for astronomical imaging with Hubble and Webb; this work ports it to gravitational waves.
Check one: does the learned noise look real?

The first thing to confirm is whether the diffusion model has actually captured the statistics of LIGO noise. The authors draw 1024 four-second synthetic noise segments, each sampled at 4096 Hz, from the trained model, compute their power spectral density, and compare it against a Welch estimate from real LIGO-Hanford data (Figure 1). The two agree closely. More strikingly, SLIC resolves the narrow, sharp spectral lines even more finely than the Welch estimate, for a simple reason: it saw 11 hours of data during training, against 1 hour for the empirical estimate. That suggests the model is learning the spectral structure of the noise, not memorizing any single stretch of data.
Check two: inject a known signal into real noise and recover it

The sharper test is end-to-end parameter estimation. The authors inject a simulated signal modeled on GW150914, with chirp mass M = 29 M⊙, symmetric mass ratio η = 0.2495, zero spins, and luminosity distance dL = 400 Mpc, into a stretch of real LIGO noise recorded after the training window and never seen by the model, and then infer all 5 of its source parameters with SLIC. As a control, they run the same inference with a standard Gaussian likelihood built from a Welch PSD.

en.caption: Figure 2. Posterior over the five recovered parameters of the injected signal: SLIC (orange) versus the standard Gaussian likelihood (blue). Contours mark the 10%, 39.35%, and 90% intervals, and the black lines show the true values. Both methods bracket the truth, but the SLIC posterior has a smaller variance. Parameters are the chirp mass M, symmetric mass ratio η, luminosity distance dL, coalescence phase ϕc, and coalescence time tc.

en.text: The result is Figure 2. To keep the comparison fair, the authors deliberately chose a glitch-free segment, so that even the Gaussian likelihood should recover the truth — and it does. Both methods recover all five true values with high credibility. That agreement matters: it calibrates SLIC against a trusted baseline and shows the learned likelihood introduces no bias. On top of that, the SLIC posterior comes out with a smaller variance, hinting at the gains to expect once the method is turned loose on genuinely non-Gaussian, glitch-contaminated data.
A few numbers

en.caption: Table 1. Key settings and results of the SLIC gravitational-wave demonstration.
rows: 11 hours of real LIGO-Hanford noise around GW150914
4096 Hz, split into 4 s segments (the true-signal segment discarded)
1024 synthetic segments; PSD matches the real data

en.text: Why it matters, and where it stops

The core message is clean: you no longer have to assume the noise is Gaussian and stationary. By learning the real noise distribution with a diffusion model and coupling it to a differentiable waveform, SLIC builds an unbiased gravitational-wave likelihood directly from detector data, and it recovers the true parameters on real LIGO noise. Compared with segment-by-segment custom data treatment, that is a more unified and more scalable path.

It is worth being honest about the boundary. This is a proof of concept, limited to 4-second, single-detector segments, and the sampler is a plain MALA — which will bottleneck on the full compact-binary problem, where the posterior lives in roughly fifteen dimensions with nontrivial structure. The authors point to three extensions already under way: longer segments to cover neutron-star signals, multi-detector models for coherent analysis, and more powerful samplers such as flowMC. With those pieces in place, machine-learning noise models could deliver fast, scalable, and unbiased inference for the flood of events expected from next-generation detectors like Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope.

zh.text: 几乎所有引力波数据分析都建立在一个方便但并不真实的假设之上：探测器噪声是高斯（Gaussian）且平稳（stationary）的。这个假设让似然函数（likelihood）变得简单、可计算，也因此支撑了过去十年绝大多数的参数估计。但真实的 LIGO、Virgo、KAGRA 并不这么温顺——它们的灵敏度随时间漂移，数据里混着被称为 glitch 的瞬态爆发，还有会缓慢游走的窄带谱线（spectral line）。
这些偏离并非小事。最著名的一次，是首个双中子星并合事件 GW170817 恰好落在了 LIGO 探测器一个响亮的 glitch 上，不得不做专门的数据处理才能分析。随着引力波天文进入批量出结果的时代，哪怕是对高斯假设的微小偏离，也会在成千上万个事件上累积成系统性偏差。

这篇来自蒙特利尔大学、Mila、Ciela 与 Flatiron 研究所的工作换了个思路：既然真实噪声很难写出解析形式，那就别再假设它，而是直接从数据里把它学出来。作者把一种叫 Score-based Likelihood Characterization（SLIC，基于分数的似然刻画）的方法引入引力波推断——用一个 score-based 扩散模型学习真实探测器噪声的分布，再与可微的物理波形模型耦合，构造出一个不依赖高斯假设的无偏似然。

zh.caption: 图1 由 SLIC 生成的合成噪声功率谱密度（PSD，蓝线）与真实 LIGO-Hanford 数据的 Welch 估计（灰色虚线）对比。蓝线取自 1024 段合成噪声，浅蓝带为 68% 置信区间。SLIC 不仅整体贴合真实噪声，还因为见过更多数据（11 小时 vs 1 小时），把窄带谱线刻画得比 Welch 更精细。

zh.text: 论文与代码：论文见 https://ml4astro.github.io/icml2023/assets/70.pdf ，代码开源在 https://github.com/RonanLegin/slicgw 。
问题：似然需要一个噪声模型，而真实噪声没有解析形式
从引力波探测器里提取天体物理信息，本质上是一个贝叶斯推断问题：给定一段数据，反推源参数（黑洞质量、自旋、距离等）的后验分布。这一步需要似然，而似然的形状完全由噪声的统计性质决定。高斯平稳假设之所以流行，正是因为它给出一个闭式的似然，算起来又快又稳。
问题在于，真实数据里的 glitch、谱线、以及阈下的天体物理信号，大多没有现成的生成模型可用。今天的做法往往是逐段做定制化处理，成本高，还可能在不经意间引入偏差。作者想要的是：保留标准推断所依赖的确定性波形模型的全部优点，同时把关于噪声的那条不现实的假设丢掉。
方法：学噪声的“分数”，而不是假设它的形状
SLIC 针对的是一类“加性噪声反问题”：观测等于一个确定性的信号模型加上噪声，即 x_O = M(θ) + x。这里 M(θ) 是由源参数 θ 决定的波形，x 是噪声。关键的观察是：如果能拿到噪声分布 Q 的分数（score，即对数概率的梯度 ∇ₓ log Q(x)），再借助波形模型对参数的雅可比（Jacobian）∇θ M(θ)，就能把似然对参数的梯度写出来：
∇θ log p(x_O | θ) = −∇ₓ log Q(x) · ∇θ M(θ)，其中 x = x_O − M(θ)。

于是方法分成两半。噪声这一半：用去噪分数匹配（denoising score matching）训练一个 score-based 扩散模型，直接从真实 LIGO 噪声样本里学出 ∇ₓ log Q(x)，完全不假设它是高斯的。物理这一半：波形用可微的 IMRPhenomD，通过 ripple 软件包实现，从而可以对它做自动微分，拿到上式需要的雅可比。两者相乘给出似然的分数后，作者用 Metropolis 调整的 Langevin 算法（MALA）从后验中采样。这个框架最初是为哈勃、韦伯的天文成像开发的，这篇工作把它迁移到了引力波。
验证一：学出来的噪声，长得像真的吗？

第一件要确认的事，是这个扩散模型是否真的学到了 LIGO 噪声的统计特征。作者从训练好的模型里采样 1024 段 4 秒长的合成噪声，计算它们的功率谱密度，再和从真实 LIGO-Hanford 数据得到的 Welch 估计对比（见图1）。两者高度吻合；更有意思的是，SLIC 甚至把噪声里那些又窄又尖的谱线刻画得比 Welch 更清楚——原因很直接：它在训练时见过 11 小时的数据，而经验估计只用了 1 小时。这说明模型不是在死记某一段噪声，而是学到了噪声的谱结构。
验证二：把已知信号注进真实噪声，能不能把参数找回来？
更关键的检验是端到端的参数估计。作者把一个 GW150914 式的模拟信号（chirp mass M = 29 M⊙，η = 0.2495，自旋为零，光度距离 dL = 400 Mpc）注入到一段训练窗口之后、模型从未见过的真实 LIGO 噪声里，然后用 SLIC 反推信号的五个参数。作为对照，他们同时用一条标准的高斯似然（基于 Welch PSD）做同样的推断。

zh.caption: 图2 注入信号五个参数的后验分布：SLIC（橙色）与标准高斯似然（蓝色）。等高线对应 10%、39.35% 与 90% 区间，黑色直线标出参数真值。两种方法都把真值包在可信区间内，但 SLIC 的后验方差更小。参数依次为啁啾质量 M、对称质量比 η、光度距离 dL、并合相位 ϕc、并合时间 tc。

zh.text: 结果如图2。为了让对照公平，作者特意选了一段没有明显 glitch 的“干净”噪声，这样连高斯似然也应当能给出正确结果。事实确实如此：两种方法都以高可信度把五个参数的真值恢复了出来。这个一致性很重要——它把 SLIC 对着一条久经检验的基线校准，证明这套学来的似然没有引入偏差。而在此之上，SLIC 的后验方差还更小一些。
几个关键数字

zh.caption: 表1 SLIC 引力波演示中的关键设定与结果。
rows: GW150914 附近 11 小时真实 LIGO-Hanford 噪声
4096 Hz，切成 4 秒片段（含真信号的片段被剔除）
采样 1024 段合成噪声，PSD 与真实数据吻合

zh.text: 意义与边界
这篇工作的核心信息很清晰：你不必再假设噪声是高斯、平稳的。用扩散模型把真实噪声分布学出来，再和可微波形耦合，SLIC 就能直接从探测器数据构造出无偏的引力波似然，并在真实 LIGO 噪声上找回了信号的真值。相比逐段定制的数据处理，这是一条更统一、也更容易扩展的路。

同时要诚实地看待它的边界：目前这还是一个概念验证，局限在 4 秒、单探测器的片段，采样器也只是简单的 MALA——面对紧致双星那种十几维、结构复杂的完整后验时，MALA 的效率会成为瓶颈。作者已经指明了三条扩展路线：把片段拉长以覆盖中子星信号，训练多探测器模型做相干分析，以及换用 flowMC 这类更强的采样器。这些拼图补齐之后，用机器学习去建模噪声，有望为下一代 Cosmic Explorer、Einstein Telescope 时代的海量事件，提供快速、可扩展且无偏的推断。

这篇来自蒙特利尔大学、Mila、Ciela 与 Flatiron 研究所的工作换了个思路：既然真实噪声很难写出解析形式，那就别再假设它，而是直接从数据里把它学出来。作者把一种叫 Score-based Likelihood Characterization（SLIC，基于分数的似然刻画）的方法引入引力波推断——用一个 score-based 扩散模型学习真实探测器噪声的分布，再与可微的物理波形模型耦合，构造出一个不依赖高斯假设的无偏似然。

zh.caption: 图1 由 SLIC 生成的合成噪声功率谱密度（PSD，蓝线）与真实 LIGO-Hanford 数据的 Welch 估计（灰色虚线）对比。蓝线取自 1024 段合成噪声，浅蓝带为 68% 置信区间。SLIC 不仅整体贴合真实噪声，还因为见过更多数据（11 小时 vs 1 小时），把窄带谱线刻画得比 Welch 更精细。

zh.title: ICML 2023 | 不再假设噪声是高斯的：用扩散模型做无偏的引力波参数估计
zh.subtitle: 蒙特利尔与 Flatiron 研究所团队提出 Score-based Likelihood Characterization（SLIC），直接从真实探测器数据里学噪声分布

en.text: The method: learn the score of the noise instead of assuming its form

SLIC targets a class of additive-noise inverse problems, where an observation equals a deterministic signal model plus noise: x_O = M(θ) + x. Here M(θ) is the waveform determined by the source parameters θ, and x is the noise. The key observation is that if you can obtain the score of the noise distribution Q — the gradient of its log-probability, ∇ₓ log Q(x) — then, combined with the Jacobian of the waveform model ∇θ M(θ), you can write the gradient of the likelihood with respect to the source parameters as the product below:
∇θ log p(x_O | θ) = −∇ₓ log Q(x) · ∇θ M(θ),  with  x = x_O − M(θ).

The method therefore splits in two. For the noise, a score-based diffusion model is trained with denoising score matching to learn ∇ₓ log Q(x) directly from samples of real LIGO noise, with no assumption that it is Gaussian. For the physics, the waveform is the differentiable IMRPhenomD model implemented in the ripple package, which makes automatic differentiation — and hence the Jacobian the equation needs — possible. Multiplying the two gives the score of the likelihood, and the authors draw posterior samples from it using a Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA). The framework was originally developed for astronomical imaging with Hubble and Webb; this work ports it to gravitational waves.
Check two: inject a known signal into real noise and recover it

The sharper test is end-to-end parameter estimation. The authors inject a simulated signal modeled on GW150914, with chirp mass M = 29 M⊙, symmetric mass ratio η = 0.2495, zero spins, and luminosity distance dL = 400 Mpc, into a stretch of real LIGO noise recorded after the training window and never seen by the model, and then infer all 5 of its source parameters with SLIC. As a control, they run the same inference with a standard Gaussian likelihood built from a Welch PSD.

en.caption: Figure 2. Posterior over the five recovered parameters of the injected signal: SLIC (orange) versus the standard Gaussian likelihood (blue). Contours mark the 10%, 39.35%, and 90% intervals, and the black lines show the true values. Both methods bracket the truth, but the SLIC posterior has a smaller variance. Parameters are the chirp mass M, symmetric mass ratio η, luminosity distance dL, coalescence phase ϕc, and coalescence time tc.

en.text: The result is Figure 2. To keep the comparison fair, the authors deliberately chose a glitch-free segment, so that even the Gaussian likelihood should recover the truth — and it does. Both methods recover all five true values with high credibility. That agreement matters: it calibrates SLIC against a trusted baseline and shows the learned likelihood introduces no bias. On top of that, the SLIC posterior comes out with a smaller variance, hinting at the gains to expect once the method is turned loose on genuinely non-Gaussian, glitch-contaminated data.

en.title: ICML 2023: Dropping the Gaussian-Noise Assumption in Gravitational-Wave Inference
en.subtitle: A Montréal and Flatiron Institute team introduces Score-based Likelihood Characterization (SLIC), learning real detector noise directly from data instead of assuming its shape.

zh.title: ICML 2023 | 不再假设噪声是高斯的：用扩散模型做无偏的引力波参数估计
zh.subtitle: 蒙特利尔与 Flatiron 研究所团队提出 Score-based Likelihood Characterization（SLIC），直接从真实探测器数据里学噪声分布

en.text: Almost all gravitational-wave data analysis rests on a convenient fiction: that detector noise is Gaussian and stationary. The assumption is what makes the likelihood tractable and cheap to evaluate, and it has underpinned most of the last decade's parameter estimation. Real instruments are less obliging. The sensitivity of LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA drifts over time, their data are peppered with transient bursts called glitches, and narrow spectral lines wander slowly across the band.

These departures are not academic. The most famous example is the first binary neutron star merger, GW170817, which landed squarely on top of a loud glitch in a LIGO detector and required bespoke data surgery before it could be analyzed. As gravitational-wave astronomy moves into an era of large event catalogs, even small deviations from the Gaussian assumption quietly accumulate into systematic biases across thousands of signals.

This work, from the Université de Montréal, Mila, Ciela, and the Flatiron Institute, takes a different route. If real noise is hard to write down in closed form, then stop assuming it and learn it from the data instead. The authors bring a technique called Score-based Likelihood Characterization (SLIC) to gravitational-wave inference: a score-based diffusion model learns the distribution of real detector noise, which is then coupled to a differentiable physical waveform model to form an unbiased likelihood that never assumes the noise is Gaussian.

en.caption: Figure 1. Power spectral density (PSD) of synthetic noise generated by SLIC (blue), compared with a Welch estimate from real LIGO-Hanford data (dashed gray). The blue curve is drawn from 1024 synthetic segments, with the light-blue band showing the 68% interval. SLIC closely matches the real noise and, having seen more data (11 h vs 1 h), resolves the narrow spectral lines even more finely than the Welch estimate.

The blue curve is drawn from 1024 synthetic segments, with the light-blue band showing the 68% interval. SLIC closely matches the real noise and, having seen more data (11 h vs 1 h), resolves the narrow spectral lines even more finely than the Welch estimate.

en.text: Why it matters, and where it stops

The core message is clean: you no longer have to assume the noise is Gaussian and stationary. By learning the real noise distribution with a diffusion model and coupling it to a differentiable waveform, SLIC builds an unbiased gravitational-wave likelihood directly from detector data, and it recovers the true parameters on real LIGO noise. Compared with segment-by-segment custom data treatment, that is a more unified and more scalable path.

It is worth being honest about the boundary. This is a proof of concept, limited to 4-second, single-detector segments, and the sampler is a plain MALA — which will bottleneck on the full compact-binary problem, where the posterior lives in roughly fifteen dimensions with nontrivial structure. The authors point to three extensions already under way: longer segments to cover neutron-star signals, multi-detector models for coherent analysis, and more powerful samplers such as flowMC. With those pieces in place, machine-learning noise models could deliver fast, scalable, and unbiased inference for the flood of events expected from next-generation detectors like Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope.

zh.text: 意义与边界
这篇工作的核心信息很清晰：你不必再假设噪声是高斯、平稳的。用扩散模型把真实噪声分布学出来，再和可微波形耦合，SLIC 就能直接从探测器数据构造出无偏的引力波似然，并在真实 LIGO 噪声上找回了信号的真值。相比逐段定制的数据处理，这是一条更统一、也更容易扩展的路。

同时要诚实地看待它的边界：目前这还是一个概念验证，局限在 4 秒、单探测器的片段，采样器也只是简单的 MALA——面对紧致双星那种十几维、结构复杂的完整后验时，MALA 的效率会成为瓶颈。作者已经指明了三条扩展路线：把片段拉长以覆盖中子星信号，训练多探测器模型做相干分析，以及换用 flowMC 这类更强的采样器。这些拼图补齐之后，用机器学习去建模噪声，有望为下一代 Cosmic Explorer、Einstein Telescope 时代的海量事件，提供快速、可扩展且无偏的推断。
